Maladaptive Strategies.value: I pretend it happened to someone else
constantly check body for signs of danger or injury

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'Survival guilt' implies a trauma context involving deaths of others or a mass-casualty/survivor scenario, which is hard to reconcile with the stated index trauma of sexual assault in the absence of any supporting items about others dying. This is a trauma-type mismatch rather than a merely unusual appraisal.

issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: 'Feeling happy or relaxed' can function as a trigger in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile: the other triggers are perfume/cologne and body pain, while threat is dominated by touch/startle/flashback phenomena and appraisals focus on emotional numbing and self-reliance. The positive-affect trigger is not impossible, but in this item set it lacks a clear clinical link and looks mismatched to the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: The flashback item is not inherently implausible for sexual assault PTSD, but in this profile the rest of the network is strongly organized around hypervigilance to touch/body danger and negative appraisals, with no memory items and no trigger-to-memory/threat linkage in the formulation. A full reliving-style flashback can coexist, but here it sits somewhat at odds with the otherwise body/startle-centered pattern and appears insufficiently supported by the surrounding items.

vignette: Mohammad, a 27-year-old Middle Eastern male and physical therapist, experienced a traumatic sexual assault while he was walking home from work one night. The event had left him with deep emotional scars and a profound sense of vulnerability that permeated his daily life. The trauma was set off by a specific scent—a cologne worn by the perpetrator—and this olfactory trigger has since become acutely potent in Mohammad’s environment. Whenever he catches a whiff of similar scents, it feels as though the assault is happening again. The smell evokes a visceral reaction that plunges him back into the fear and helplessness he felt on that night. In addition to the scent triggers, physical pain also serves as a potent reminder. Any sensation in his body can quickly escalate into a full-blown panic attack. This somatic trigger has made it difficult for Mohammad to engage in any form of physical activity or intimacy with his wife. He feels like he’s carrying a heavy burden that isolates him from the world and from her. Mohammad had come to believe that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again, leading him to distance himself emotionally even from those close to him. The assault had left him feeling ashamed of his body and convinced that he couldn’t rely on himself in a crisis. These negative appraisals have significantly impacted how he perceives the world around him. The negative beliefs about himself have made Mohammad jumpy and easily startled, reacting with alarm at unexpected movements or touch from others. He often finds himself on high alert, constantly scanning his environment for signs of danger. This hyper-vigilance has extended to his work as a physical therapist, where he avoids touching patients and is particularly wary when they are in close proximity. Mohammad’s dissociative response—pretending the event happened to someone else—has only served to reinforce his negative appraisals and triggers. The more he dissociates, the less able he feels to trust himself or navigate the world without reliving the trauma. This maladaptive strategy has led him to avoid thinking about the assault altogether, which in turn amplifies his sensitivity to triggers. The cycle of fear and avoidance has tightened over time, making it increasingly difficult for Mohammad to function normally. His constant body monitoring and checking for signs of danger have become an exhausting routine that only heightens his startle response and feelings of vulnerability. His wife has noticed a significant change in him and is concerned about the distance he’s putting between them. The trauma has disrupted their intimate relationship, leaving both feeling isolated and hurt. Mohammad’s avoidance behaviors have also affected his work; he often finds himself distracted and unable to fully engage with patients. What finally brought Mohammad to seek help was a recent incident where he had a panic attack in front of his colleagues at the physical therapy clinic. He realized that if he didn’t address these issues, they would continue to erode every aspect of his life. The most frightening prospect for him is losing control and being unable to function as both a husband and a professional. Mohammad hopes that with help, he can reclaim some sense of normalcy and reconnect with the world around him without constantly feeling like danger lurks in every shadow and scent.
